about.title: La Palma Slip & Fall Claims
about.longDescription: Slip and fall cases in a small city like La Palma often come down to a single question: did the property owner know about the hazard, or should they have, and did they fail to act? That could be a wet floor at a shop near Walker Street, a broken stair rail at an apartment complex, or uneven pavement in a lot off La Palma Avenue. Because La Palma is compact, many falls happen at retail centers, gyms, or residential complexes shared by neighbors — places with security cameras that may only retain footage for days or weeks. California law requires proof the owner had notice of the danger, so acting quickly to document conditions and request video preservation matters. LawProactive doesn't practice law or promise results; we simply connect you with an independent attorney who can evaluate your fall, explain your options, and work on contingency so you owe nothing upfront.

whyChoose.title: Why Talk to an Attorney Quickly

items.title: Notice Has to Be Proven
items.desc: California requires showing the owner knew or reasonably should have known about the hazard and failed to fix or warn about it. An attorney can help gather maintenance logs, prior complaints, or inspection records that establish that notice.

items.title: Video Disappears Fast
items.desc: Surveillance footage from stores, complexes, or lots is often overwritten within days. Early legal help can mean a prompt request to preserve that footage before it's gone.

items.title: Comparative Fault Can Reduce, Not Erase, Your Claim
items.desc: Even if you were partly distracted or moving quickly, California's pure comparative fault rule still allows recovery reduced by your share of fault — it doesn't automatically bar your claim.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip and fall claim in La Palma?
items.answer: Generally you have two years from the date of the fall under California law. If the property involved is owned by a public entity — such as a city building — the deadline is much shorter and requires an early administrative claim. Speaking with an attorney soon after the fall helps make sure you don't miss either deadline.

items.question: What if I fell at a store or complex near La Palma Avenue and no one wrote up a report?
items.answer: A missing incident report doesn't end your claim, but it does make documentation more important. Photos of the hazard, witness names, and a prompt request for surveillance video can help fill that gap. An independent attorney can help you gather this evidence even without a formal report on file.

items.question: Do I need to prove the property owner knew about the hazard?
items.answer: Yes — California premises liability generally requires showing the owner knew, or reasonably should have known, about the dangerous condition and failed to address it in time. This is often established through maintenance records, prior complaints, or how long the hazard existed before your fall. An attorney can help investigate what the owner knew and when.
